title: Should chimps be used for medical testing?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine whether chimpanzees should be used in medical and behavioral research. They open with the story of Wenka (Winkle in the transcript), a chimp at the Yerkes Primate Institute who has been used in research since birth and is considered possibly the oldest captive primate still used in research. They trace the history of animal rights laws, the Air Force's use of chimps in space and g-force testing, the captive breeding program after CITES (1975), the AIDS/HIV chimp studies, and the 1966 Animal Welfare Act. They discuss the Coulston Foundation's abuses and its 2002 shutdown, with many chimps moving to Save the Chimps, and the Chimp Act of 2000. They close by noting that the NIH suspended new chimp biomedical and behavioral research grants in December 2011, leaving the US and Gabon as the only countries still doing biomedical chimp testing. The episode ends with a Kiva lending team listener-mail segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and chimp fondness
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about a chimp that held Josh's hand and Chuck's wish for a pet chimp, then discuss slang.

segments.title: Wenka's life story
segments.summary: The hosts tell the story of Wenka, a chimp born in 1954 whose mother died after being poisoned and who lost her infant daughter with Down syndrome, then note she has been used in research since being at Yerkes and is possibly the oldest captive primate still used in research.

segments.title: Early behavioral experiments and animal rights history
segments.summary: They describe harsh early behavioral experiments on young chimps and compare them with human studies, then trace the history of animal rights from Jeremy Bentham and early British anti-cruelty laws to the ASPCA in 1866 and the Peter Singer era.

segments.title: Genetic similarity and the case for chimp research
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how chimps are genetically close to humans, with the caveat that DNA similarity figures are often misstated, and how chimps were used in research for vaccines, hepatitis, contraceptives and addiction after human prisoner testing ended.

segments.title: Air Force space testing, CITES and captive breeding
segments.summary: The Air Force used chimps in space and rocket sled testing. After CITES in 1975 restricted wild capture, the chimp population was bred in captivity, and many current chimps descend from the original imported animals. Yerkes' earlier breeding program is also noted.

segments.title: HIV/AIDS chimp studies and the Animal Welfare Act
segments.summary: The NIH's captive breeding program and HIV/AIDS research in the 1980s led to chimps being infected with HIV, but chimps did not develop full-blown AIDS. The 1966 Animal Welfare Act set minimum care standards, and the hosts discuss the costs and the number of chimps the government was responsible for.

segments.title: Coulston Foundation abuses and the Chimp Act
segments.summary: The Coulston Foundation's toxicology work and alleged abuses of chimps are described, including the 2002 shutdown and the move of chimps to Save the Chimps. The Chimp Act of 2000 required lifetime care for retired federally funded research chimps. The Project X film and Bob Barker controversy are mentioned.

segments.title: Global chimp testing and NIH suspension of grants
segments.summary: The hosts say the US and Gabon are the only countries still doing biomedical chimp testing, list countries that have banned it, and describe the NIH's December 2011 suspension of new grants for great ape research, with hepatitis as a possible remaining use. They discuss sanctuaries and the Great Ape Project.

segments.title: Kiva lending team listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts promote the Stuff You Should Know Kiva team's drive to reach a million dollars in loans by the end of March and invite listeners to join.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and share a link to the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
